title: How to Plan an Etosha Safari Around the Waterholes
meta_title: Etosha Safari: Camps, Fees, Seasons and Routes
meta_description: Plan an Etosha safari: which camps to book, how many nights, park fees, the best months and how game drives work at the waterholes.
excerpt: An Etosha safari explained: where to stay, how many nights to give each side of the park, current park fees and when the waterholes are busiest.
content:
An Etosha safari is built around waterholes rather than long searches through the bush. Etosha National Park covers 22,270 km² of northern Namibia around a vast salt pan, and in the dry months of May to October elephants, lions, black rhinos, giraffes and big herds of springbok and zebra walk in to drink where you can sit and watch.

The catch is that Etosha is big, the camps are far apart and the park runs on strict sunrise-to-sunset rules, so a badly planned Etosha safari means hours on gravel and little time at the water. This guide covers the camps, gates, fees, seasons and how many nights to give each part of the park, from our safari team in Nairobi.

Photo by Bernd 📷 Dittrich on Unsplash

Quick Facts

  • Size: 22,270 km², with the Etosha Pan covering about 4,760 km² (around a quarter of the park)
  • Location: Northern Namibia; Halali camp is about 451 km and Namutoni about 486 km by road from Windhoek
  • Wildlife: About 114 mammal species and around 340 bird species, including black rhino, lion, elephant, leopard and cheetah
  • Best months: May to October (dry season), when animals rely on the waterholes
  • Park fee: N$280 per non-SADC foreign adult per day, plus N$60 per car per day (checked October 2026)
  • Gate hours: Sunrise to sunset; you must be inside a camp or out of the park by sunset
  • Suggested stay: 3 to 4 nights to cover the park from west to east

What Makes an Etosha Safari Different?

An Etosha safari differs from East African safaris because the landscape is flat, open and dry, and wildlife gathers at springs and boreholes instead of rivers. You drive between waterholes, switch off the engine and let the animals come to you, which makes it one of the most relaxed safaris in Africa.

Etosha was first proclaimed a game reserve in 1907 and became a national park in 1967. Its centrepiece is the Etosha Pan, a white, shimmering clay depression that is dry for most of the year. Around its edge you find grassland, low thorn scrub and, further east, mopane woodland, so the scenery changes noticeably as you cross the park.

The other big difference is how much of an Etosha safari you can do on your own. Roads are graded gravel, distances are clearly signposted and the rest camps are run by the state-owned Namibia Wildlife Resorts, so Etosha suits both self-drivers and guided travellers. Where it does not shine is off-road driving and walking: you stay in your vehicle on marked roads, and there is no bush walking inside the park.

Which animals can you see in Etosha?

An Etosha safari is best known for elephants, lions and black rhinos at the waterholes, alongside giraffe, plains zebra, blue wildebeest, gemsbok (oryx), springbok, red hartebeest and black-faced impala. Leopard and cheetah are present but harder to find, and spotted hyena and black-backed jackal are common around the camps after dark. There are no buffalo or hippo, so Etosha does not offer a full Big Five.

Where Should You Stay on an Etosha Safari?

The best base for most Etosha safari plans is a split stay: Okaukuejo in the south-west and Namutoni in the east, with Halali in the middle if you have time. All three are Namibia Wildlife Resorts camps inside the park with floodlit waterholes, so the viewing continues after the gates close.

Camp or areaWhere it isWhat it suits
OkaukuejoSouth-west, about 17 km inside the southern (Andersson) entranceFirst nights, the most famous floodlit waterhole, lions, elephants and black rhinos at night
HalaliCentre of the park, below a dolomite hill among mopane treesBreaking up the drive, leopard chances, guided morning, afternoon and night drives
NamutoniEast, in a German fort built in 1897, near the Von Lindequist GateHistory, the floodlit King Nehale waterhole and birding at nearby Fischer's Pan
Onguma Nature ReservePrivate reserve on the eastern boundary, just outside the Von Lindequist GateTravellers who want private lodges and camps, with quick access to the Namutoni side

Okaukuejo is the classic first stop on an Etosha safari, with waterhole chalets, bush chalets, double rooms and a campsite, plus a restaurant, pool and filling station, according to Namibia Wildlife Resorts. Its waterhole is a short walk from the rooms, so you can watch elephants and rhinos drink from a bench after dinner.

Halali is the quietest of the three main camps and makes sense on a four-night trip, because it cuts the long middle stretch in half. Namutoni feels different again: the whitewashed fort, the greener woodland and the birdlife around Fischer's Pan give the eastern side its own character, and it is the natural exit point if you are heading on to the Caprivi or Botswana.

Inside the park or outside the gates?

Inside the park, you trade some polish for location: you wake up at the waterhole and you are already in the game-viewing area when the camp gate opens. Outside, private reserves on the boundary offer more intimate lodges and their own activities, but you queue at the gate each morning and must leave by sunset. Many of our guests mix the two on one Etosha safari, starting inside and ending at a private lodge.

How Many Nights Should You Spend in Etosha?

Three to four nights suits most Etosha safari itineraries. Two nights works as a quick stop on a wider Namibia loop but shows you only one side of the park. Four nights lets you cross from Okaukuejo to Namutoni slowly, with dawn and late-afternoon time at the waterholes.

The park is wide rather than deep: the main road follows the southern edge of the pan for well over a hundred kilometres between the western and eastern camps. At the 50 km/h limit, with stops at every waterhole worth a look, that crossing easily fills a full day, so it pays to split it.

NightBaseWhat you do
Night 1OkaukuejoDrive up from Windhoek, enter at the Andersson Gate, afternoon game drive, evening at the floodlit waterhole
Night 2OkaukuejoFull day on the western and southern waterholes and the pan edge; dusk back at camp
Night 3HalaliSlow drive east along the pan, stopping at waterholes; optional guided night drive
Night 4Namutoni or OngumaEastern waterholes and Fischer's Pan, then exit through the Von Lindequist Gate the next morning

If you have only two nights for your Etosha safari, stay both at Okaukuejo or both on the eastern side and accept that you will not see the whole park. Our 7-day Classic Etosha National Park safari goes the other way, staying inside the park the whole time and moving through the southern, central and eastern camps, which suits travellers who care most about wildlife. If you want the dunes as well, the 5-day Sossusvlei and Etosha tour combines both highlights in a short trip.

When Is the Best Time for an Etosha Safari?

The best time for an Etosha safari is the dry season from May to October. With little water left in the bush, animals depend on the waterholes, the grass is short and visibility is excellent. The rainy season from November to April is lush and wonderful for birds, but wildlife spreads out and sightings take more patience.

Photo by Eelco Böhtlingk on Unsplash

MonthsSeasonWhat to expect in Etosha
May to JulyEarly dry season, coolMild days and cold early mornings, game starting to gather at waterholes, fewer crowds than later in the year
August to OctoberLate dry seasonPeak waterhole action and dust; the busiest period, so book camps inside the park well ahead
November to DecemberEarly rainsHeat and building storms, first green flush, game begins to disperse; migrant birds arrive
January to AprilRainy seasonGreen landscape, newborn antelope, excellent birding; the pan can hold water after good rains, but sightings are less predictable

Our honest advice: if this is your first Etosha safari and wildlife is the priority, aim for June to September. If you have already done the dry season or love birds and photography of green landscapes, the rains can be rewarding. For the rest of the country month by month, see our guide to the best time to visit Namibia, and for a feel of the rainy season read what Namibia is like in January.

How Much Does It Cost to Enter Etosha?

Entering Etosha costs N$280 per person per day for adults from outside the SADC region, plus N$60 per day for a car with 10 seats or fewer, under the Government Gazette fee schedule in force from 1 April 2026 (checked October 2026). Older guides quoting lower figures are out of date.

VisitorDaily feeNotes
Foreign adult (non-SADC, 16+)N$280Park entrance plus conservation fee
SADC adult (16+)N$180Citizens of Southern African Development Community countries
Foreign child (9 to 15)N$180SADC children of the same age pay N$100
Child aged 8 or underFreeAll nationalities
Vehicle, 10 seats or fewerN$60Per vehicle per day

As a worked example, two non-SADC adults spending three days in Etosha in their own car would pay 2 x N$280 x 3 plus N$60 x 3, which is N$1,860 in park fees. On a guided Etosha safari these fees are normally built into your quote, so ask whether they are included. Accommodation, guided drives and transport are the larger costs, and they vary widely between rest-camp rooms and private lodges.

How Do Game Drives Work in Etosha?

Game drives on an Etosha safari are slow loops between waterholes, from sunrise when the camp gates open until you are back in camp before sunset. You can drive yourself, join a rest-camp guided drive or travel with a private guide; choosing a few waterholes and waiting beats rushing between them.

Photo by Sergi Ferrete on Unsplash

The rules are simple and strictly enforced: stay inside your vehicle except at fenced camps and designated toilet stops, keep to the marked roads, and drive at 50 km/h or less. Turning off the engine at a waterhole is good manners and gives you better sightings, because animals relax when the noise stops.

Halali and Namutoni both list guided morning, afternoon and night drives. Night drives are the only way on an Etosha safari to be out in the park after dark, and they give you a chance at hyena, honey badger, owls and sometimes rhino or lion on the move. Book them at reception as soon as you arrive, because places are limited.

Self-drive or guided Etosha safari?

A self-drive Etosha safari gives you freedom and costs less, and the roads are manageable in an ordinary car in the dry season. A guided Etosha safari adds a trained spotter, local knowledge of which waterholes are active this week and no stress about gate times or fuel. We compare the two in detail in our post on guided Namibia safaris versus self-drive.

What Is the Etosha Pan Like?

The Etosha Pan is a flat, white salt pan of about 4,760 km², roughly a quarter of the park. For most of the year it is dry and cracked, with heat haze on the horizon. After a good rainy season parts of it hold shallow water and can attract flamingos and other waterbirds.

Photo by Eelco Böhtlingk on Unsplash

You cannot drive onto the pan itself except at a few designated viewpoints, but roads along its southern edge give you wide views across it. The open grassland at the edge of the pan is where you are most likely to find ostrich, springbok and gemsbok, often with lions resting nearby. In the late afternoon the low sun turns the pan edge pale gold, which is one of the best times for photographs on an Etosha safari.

Insider Tips

  • Book early: Camps inside the park fill up for July to October, so reserve as soon as your dates are firm
  • Arrive before sunset: Gate times follow the sun; allow plenty of margin, because you cannot drive in the park after dark
  • Fill up: Fuel up at the camps or in Outjo or Tsumeb before long drives; distances inside the park add up
  • Wait at the water: The best Etosha safari sightings come from choosing two or three waterholes and sit for 30 to 60 minutes rather than racing between them
  • Sit up at night: Take a warm layer to the floodlit waterhole; the cold dry-season nights are often when rhinos come to drink
  • Bring binoculars: Animals on the pan edge can be far away, and binoculars make a huge difference

How Do You Get to Etosha National Park?

Most travellers start an Etosha safari by road from Windhoek, a long drive north. Halali sits about 451 km and Namutoni about 486 km from the capital by road, and the route to the southern side via Outjo is tarred to Okaukuejo. Some private lodges on the boundary, such as Onguma, have airstrips for charter flights.

There are four entrances: the Andersson Gate in the south near Okaukuejo, the Von Lindequist Gate in the east near Namutoni, the Galton Gate in the west and the King Nehale Gate in the north. Onguma describes its reserve as about five and a half hours by road from Windhoek's Hosea Kutako International Airport, which is a fair guide to the eastern side.

Because of the distances, most people break the trip with a night on the way, often near Otjiwarongo or Outjo. If you are new to driving in Namibia, read our list of first-time Namibia safari mistakes before you go; underestimating gravel-road driving time is the most common one.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many days do you need for an Etosha National Park safari?

An Etosha safari needs at least two nights to be worthwhile and three or four nights to cross the park from Okaukuejo in the south-west to Namutoni in the east. Two nights suit a stop on a wider Namibia loop; four nights let you spend dawn and dusk at different waterholes without long daily drives.

How much is the Etosha entrance fee?

The Etosha entrance fee for non-SADC foreign adults is N$280 per person per day, plus N$60 per day for a vehicle with 10 seats or fewer (Government Gazette fee schedule in force from 1 April 2026, checked October 2026). SADC adults pay N$180, children aged 8 and under enter free, and fees should be confirmed before you travel.

When is the best time for an Etosha safari?

The best time for an Etosha safari is the dry season from May to October, when surface water dries up and animals gather at the waterholes, so sightings are easier and more reliable. The rainy months from November to April turn Etosha green and bring migrant birds, but game spreads out and some tracks can be affected by rain.

Can you self-drive in Etosha National Park?

Yes, you can self-drive an Etosha safari on the park's gravel roads in an ordinary car during the dry season, as long as you stay in your vehicle, keep to marked roads, drive at 50 km/h or less and reach your camp before the gates close at sunset. A guided safari adds a spotter, local knowledge of recent sightings and no navigation stress.

Is it better to stay inside or outside Etosha?

Staying inside the park on an Etosha safari puts you at a floodlit waterhole after dark and at the first game-viewing spots as soon as the camp gates open at sunrise. Staying outside, on a private reserve such as Onguma beside the Von Lindequist Gate, usually means quieter, more polished lodges, but you lose time driving in each morning.

Final Thoughts

A good Etosha safari is less about covering ground and more about being at the right waterhole at the right hour. Give it three or four nights, go between May and October if wildlife comes first, split your stay between the western and eastern camps, and keep an evening free for the floodlit waterhole.
